answer.evidence: The object is a tiny cluster of snowy rocks about 9 rows tall. The snow caps are 1-2 white rows (rows 6-7, 10-11) sitting on dark grey faces of about 2-3 rows (rows 12-13). The snow reads as a thin highlight, not a horizontal surface, and there is no front-edge line with eave shadow. Silhouette widths go from 12 at rows 10-11 to 10 and then 6, a plain tapering mound with no ellipse. The top is a rim of 2 rows at most and the front face is under 3 rows, so it reads as a front elevation rather than a three-quarter view.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny snowy rock cluster, roughly 10x8 px, shown beside two full trees. It is smaller than one 16x16 tile, so the per-tile facts read 0 and I judged by eye. By eye it has about 3 steps (white highlight, light grey, mid grey) with only a few pixels of shadow, against 5-6+ steps and many leaf clumps in the references. Its dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, so the outline is a neutral grey or black line and not a tinted material tone, while both references measure 0% neutral. There is almost no grain, speckle or per-stone shading. The piece is too small and sparse to judge reliably, and nothing in it matches the references' richness, so it looks thinner and more sticker-like. The reference kind is also a canopy tree, which is a poor match for a rock prop. When in doubt, fail.
